tr.en: Teahouses have over a thousand years of history in China. In the past they were not only places to drink tea and rest but important places for getting information: merchants did business there, scholars exchanged learning, ordinary people listened to stories and chatted about family matters. A teahouse was a small society. As the pace of life quickened, traditional teahouses went quiet for a time. But in recent years new-style teahouses have sprung up one after another in big cities. While keeping traditional tea culture, they add modern design and things young people like, such as creative tea drinks and book-sharing events, attracting large numbers of young customers. Experts think their popularity reflects young people's rediscovery of, and love for, traditional culture.

tr.en: Many think how good your memory is is settled in childhood. But psychological research finds memory isn't unchangeable: it can be improved by scientific methods. Linking what you need to remember with familiar images, for instance, is a very effective memory technique. A memory-competition champion once explained that he imagines the numbers to remember as vivid little stories, so that even long afterwards he can recall them accurately. Enough sleep matters a great deal too: research shows that during sleep the brain sorts and consolidates the day's information, so cramming late at night often works badly.

tr.en: In big cities where land is very tight, building a large park isn't easy. So "pocket parks" appeared. A pocket park is a small open space in the city. They aren't big — some only a few hundred square metres — but they are spread beside housing blocks and on street corners, a few minutes' walk from people's doors. Small as they are, they lack nothing: besides grass and benches there are fitness facilities and children's play equipment. In the morning old people practise tai chi there; in the evening children run around playing. More importantly, pocket parks are usually built on small spare plots, which both saves land and improves the surroundings. Some cities, for example, have turned disused car parks into pocket parks, so that once dirty, messy corners have become clean and attractive. Experts point out that the key is meeting people's needs: in planning, the views of nearby residents should be fully heard, so that the park truly becomes somewhere residents want to go and can use.

tr.en: Twenty-eight-year-old Li Xin restores old books. Every day she sits at her workbench and, with all kinds of small tools and brushes, mends damaged old books bit by bit. She has kept at this work for six years. At university she studied history. By chance she visited the library's book-restoration room, and from that moment she was deeply drawn to the work. After graduating she turned down high salaries from several companies and chose this poorly paid job. Restoring old books takes enormous patience: a badly damaged page can take several days, and a complete old book may take years. When she started, Li Xin was upset for days over a small mistake; it was her master's words, "Take your time — the book isn't in a hurry", that calmed her down. Now she has restored over a hundred old books on her own. "Every book I mend is like bringing a piece of history back to life. I feel what I do is very meaningful."

tr.en: After dark, the other side of the city is just beginning. Night markets, late-night bookshops, 24-hour convenience stores, light shows — ever richer night-time spending makes up what is now called the "night economy". It generally means service consumption between six in the evening and six the next morning. Figures show that in some big cities night-time spending is over half of the whole day's. Its growth meets residents' varied needs and creates many jobs. To draw more people out at night, many cities have taken measures: longer metro and bus hours, more night lighting, museums open in the evening. Some have even set up a "night-time district head" to coordinate everything related to the night economy. But its fast growth also brings noise, traffic jams and more rubbish. How to balance a thriving economy with residents' rest is a question city managers must think hard about.

tr.en: For a long time people thought plants were quiet, passive life. But more and more research finds that plants do "communicate". Scientists have observed that when insects eat a tree's leaves, it releases a special gas. Nearby trees that "smell" it produce substances insects dislike in their own leaves in advance, protecting themselves — as if the injured tree were warning its neighbours, "Careful, danger!" Besides the air, plants can also "pass on messages" through their roots. In forest soil live huge numbers of tiny organisms that link the roots of different plants into a vast underground network. Through it, big trees can send nutrients to small trees growing beneath them without enough sunlight, and sick plants can send signals to those around them. Some scientists vividly call it the "forest internet". Of course plant "communication" is quite unlike human language: plants have no consciousness and don't think. But these findings remind us that the plant world is far more complex than we imagine.

items.text:
过去，人们一直认为植物是安静的、被动的生命。然而，越来越多的研究发现，植物之间其实也存在着“交流”。
科学家观察到，当一棵树的叶子被昆虫吃掉时，它会释放出一种特殊的气体。附近的树“闻”到这种气体后，会提前在叶子里产生昆虫讨厌的物质，从而保护自己不受伤害。这就好像受伤的树在提醒周围的同伴：“小心，有危险！”
除了通过空气，植物还能通过地下的根“传递消息”。在森林的土壤中，生活着大量很小的生物，它们把不同植物的根连接起来，形成了一张巨大的地下网络。通过这张网络，大树可以把营养输送给长在它下面、缺少阳光的小树，生病的植物也能向周围的植物发出信号。有科学家形象地把它称为“森林互联网”。
当然，植物的“交流”和人类的语言完全不同，它们没有意识，也不会思考。但这些发现提醒我们，植物的世界远比我们想象的复杂。

tr.en: Thirty-two-year-old Zhang Wei was a product manager at an internet company in Shanghai, well paid with a bright future. But three years ago he made a decision that surprised everyone: he quit and went home to Yunnan to grow coffee. His home in southern Yunnan has a climate and soil well suited to coffee, but for a long time local farmers sold their beans cheaply to buyers and earned little. "Our coffee is actually very good — we just have no brand of our own," he says. Back home, he learnt growing and processing from experts while using his internet experience to open an online shop and livestream the story of his home's coffee. At first orders were few, and some even mocked him for giving up a good job to be a farmer. But he didn't give up. In the second year his coffee won a prize in a national competition, and orders shot up. Now he has brought over fifty village households into growing coffee with him, and their incomes have more than doubled. "I hope one day, when people mention good coffee, they'll think of my home."

三十二岁的张伟曾经是上海一家互联网公司的产品经理，收入很高，前途光明。然而三年前，他做出了一个让所有人意外的决定：辞职回到云南老家种植咖啡。
张伟的家乡位于云南南部，气候和土壤都非常适合种植咖啡。但过去很长时间，当地农民只是把咖啡低价卖给收购的人，自己赚不到多少钱。“我们这里的咖啡品质其实很好，只是没有自己的品牌。”张伟说。
回乡后，张伟一边向专家学习种植和加工技术，一边利用自己在互联网行业积累的经验，在网上开店、直播，讲述家乡咖啡的故事。起初，订单很少，甚至有人笑他“放着好好的工作不做，回来当农民”。但他没有放弃。第二年，他的咖啡在一次全国比赛中得了奖，订单一下子多了起来。
如今，张伟已经带动了村里五十多户农民和他一起种植咖啡，大家的收入比过去增加了一倍多。谈到未来，张伟说：“我希望有一天，人们一提到好咖啡，就会想到我们的家乡。”

tr.en: At every holiday, famous sights are packed: queuing for hours and seeing only the backs of heads is common. So a style called "reverse tourism" has become popular with young people. It means avoiding popular cities and sights and travelling to small, less-known towns with few people. Online, many young people share their experiences: strolling slowly through a small town, tasting authentic snacks, chatting with locals… Such trips cost less, they say, yet feel more real and relaxing. The trend has also brought small towns opportunities: some have seized them, improving transport and accommodation and discovering and promoting local culture, drawing more and more visitors. But experts warn that while developing tourism, small towns must protect their original way of life and avoid over-commercialisation, or they'll lose the unique charm that attracts visitors.

每到节假日，有名的景点总是到处都是人，排队几个小时、只能看人头的情况并不少见。于是，一种被称为“反向旅游”的方式在年轻人中流行了起来。
反向旅游就是避开热门城市和景点，选择那些人少、不太有名的小城市出游。在网上，不少年轻人分享了自己的反向旅游经历：在小城里慢慢散步，品尝地道的小吃，和当地人聊天……他们说，这样的旅行花费更少，体验却更真实、更放松。
反向旅游的流行，也给一些小城市带来了发展机遇。有的地方抓住机会，改善交通和住宿条件，发现并宣传本地的特色文化，吸引了越来越多的游客。不过，也有专家提醒，小城市在发展旅游的同时，要注意保护原有的生活方式，避免过度商业化，否则就会失去吸引游客的独特魅力。

tr.en: You open the wardrobe — it's stuffed with clothes, yet you feel there's nothing to wear; you own more and more, yet life isn't any happier for it. Many people have felt this, which is why in recent years the idea of "minimalist living" has won more and more support. Minimalism doesn't mean wanting nothing, but keeping only what you truly need and truly love. Its advocates believe the fewer things you have, the less time and energy you spend sorting and choosing, so you can focus on what matters. You can usually start by sorting your belongings: some suggest that anything unused for over a year can be dealt with — given to someone who needs it, donated or recycled. More importantly, before buying, ask yourself, "Do I really need this?" Note that minimalism is an attitude, not a standard. Everyone's needs differ, and there's no need to throw things away deliberately for the sake of it. What suits you is best.

打开柜子，满满都是衣服，却总觉得没有衣服可穿；家里的东西越来越多，生活却并没有因此变得更快乐。这样的感受，相信很多人都有过。正因为如此，近年来，“简单生活”的理念得到了越来越多人的认同。
简单生活并不意味着什么都不要，而是只保留真正需要和真正喜欢的东西。提倡这种生活方式的人认为，物品越少，花在整理和选择上的时间和精力就越少，人就能把更多的注意力放在重要的事情上。
实践简单生活，通常可以从整理物品开始。有人建议，对于一年以上没有用过的东西，就可以考虑处理掉——送给需要的人、捐出去或者回收利用。更重要的是，在购物之前多问自己一句：“我真的需要它吗？”
值得注意的是，简单生活是一种态度，而不是一种标准。每个人的需要不同，不必为了“简单”而故意扔掉东西。适合自己的，才是最好的。

tr.en: Paper-cutting is one of China's oldest folk arts. With a pair of scissors and a sheet of red paper, in a paper-cutter's hands it quickly becomes lively flowers, birds, fish and insects. In the past, at every Spring Festival, people pasted paper-cuts on their windows to express good wishes for the new year. Paper-cutting looks simple but demands great skill: the cutter needs not only a good grounding but rich imagination to turn all kinds of scenes from life into patterns on paper. As times changed, this traditional art once faced the danger of disappearing. To pass it on, many places have opened paper-cutting classes and combined it with modern design, making new products young people like.

tr.en: You may not expect it, but four hundred kilometres above the earth, astronauts can grow vegetables. On China's space station researchers have carried out growing experiments with several plants in turn; lettuce and tomatoes have grown successfully. Growing plants in space isn't easy: without gravity, roots don't know which way to grow, and water doesn't naturally flow downwards. So scientists designed special growing equipment, replacing sunlight with lamps and precisely controlling temperature and humidity to create the right environment. The experiments can not only supply fresh vegetables for astronauts living long in space in future but also help scientists better grasp the laws of plant growth; the results may one day be applied to farming on earth.

在太空种植物并不容易。由于没有重力，植物的根不知道该往哪个方向长，水也不会（　）地往下流。为此，科学家专门设计了特殊的种植设备，用灯光代替阳光，并通过精确地（　）温度和湿度，为植物创造合适的生长环境。
这些实验不仅能为将来宇航员在太空中长期生活提供新鲜蔬菜，还能帮助科学家更好地（　）植物生长的规律。研究成果将来也有可能（　）到地球上的农业生产中。

tr.en: On the streets of some cities there's a special post office: the "time post office". Unlike an ordinary post office, letters sent here take a long time to arrive: you can write a letter here and choose to have it sent one, five or even ten years later. Many people write to their future selves. Some write down their worries of the moment — years later, reading them again, they may find those worries were nothing at all; some write down their dreams, hoping to realise them. Others write to family and friends, putting on paper what they can't usually bring themselves to say. A member of staff says the letter that moved her most was a father's: he wrote it on the day his daughter was born, arranging for it to arrive on her eighteenth birthday. In an age that chases speed in everything, the time post office makes people slow down. Perhaps waiting is itself something beautiful.

tr.en: Sixty-five-year-old Teacher Wang taught maths at a secondary school before retiring. After retiring she didn't sit idle. Seeing that many old people on her estate couldn't use smartphones — even booking a hospital appointment or paying bills had become hard — she decided to run a free "phone class". Every Wednesday evening she teaches them in the estate's activity room. When she meets complicated steps, she turns them into short, easy-to-remember sentences to help everyone remember. Some learn slowly and ask the same question several times, but she never finds it a bother and always explains again and again patiently. Six months on, over a hundred old people have learnt to video-chat with family and pay bills online. An eighty-year-old woman said happily, "I always felt I couldn't keep up with the times; now I'm finally not afraid." Teacher Wang says teaching old people to use phones isn't only teaching them a skill; more importantly, it lets them feel cared for.

tr.en: Many Chinese cities have large numbers of old estates built twenty or thirty years ago. Most of their buildings have only six or seven floors and were built without lifts. As residents age, getting up and down stairs has become a daily problem for many old people. "I live on the fifth floor and my legs are bad; every time I come back from shopping I have to rest several times on the stairs," says 72-year-old Aunt Liu. To solve this, in recent years many places have started fitting lifts in old estates. But it isn't simple. First there's cost: installing one lift often costs hundreds of thousands of yuan — who pays? Second, opinions are hard to unite: residents on high floors mostly support it, while those on the first and second floors worry a lift will block their light and bring noise, while they themselves won't use it. So some places have found a way: the government gives a subsidy, and residents share the rest by floor — the higher the floor, the more they pay. Meanwhile community workers visit door to door again and again to listen patiently to all sides. With everyone's effort, Aunt Liu's building finally got a lift. "Going out is so much easier now — I can go dancing in the park every day again!"

items.text:
在中国很多城市，都有大量二三十年前建成的老小区。这些小区的楼大多只有六七层，当初建设时没有安装电梯。随着居民年龄越来越大，上下楼成了许多老人每天都要面对的难题。“我住在五楼，腿不好，每次买菜回来都得在楼梯上休息好几次。”七十二岁的刘阿姨说。
为了解决这个问题，近年来，各地开始推动老小区加装电梯。不过，这件事做起来并不简单。首先是费用问题：一部电梯的安装费用往往需要几十万元，由谁来出钱？其次是意见很难统一：住在高层的居民大多支持，而住在一二楼的居民则担心电梯会挡住阳光、带来噪声，自己却用不上。
为此，一些地方想出了办法：政府给一定的补贴，剩下的费用由居民按楼层共同承担，楼层越高，出的钱越多。同时，社区工作人员一次次上门沟通，耐心听取各方的意见。
在大家的共同努力下，刘阿姨家的楼终于装上了电梯。“现在出门方便多了，我又能天天去公园跳舞了！”

tr.en: Every autumn tens of thousands of migratory birds fly from the cold north to the warm south for the winter, and fly back the next spring. Some cover over ten thousand kilometres in one journey and find the same place accurately year after year. How do they do it? Long research has found their way-finding comes from several sources. First, they judge direction by the sun and stars: the sun by day, the stars by night. Second, many can sense the earth's magnetic field, as if carrying a "compass" inside them. Besides, landmarks on the ground — rivers, mountains, coasts — help them confirm where they are. But in recent years their long journeys face more and more challenges: city lights at night make birds flying in the dark lose their way, and the loss of waterside grassland deprives them of places to rest and find food on the way. Protecting migratory birds needs everyone's effort.

items.text:
每年秋天，成千上万只候鸟会从寒冷的北方飞往温暖的南方过冬，第二年春天再飞回来。有的候鸟一次飞行的距离有一万多公里，而且年年都能准确地找到同一个地方。它们是怎么做到的呢？
科学家经过长期研究发现，候鸟找路的本领来自多个方面。首先，它们能利用太阳和星星的位置来判断方向：白天看太阳，晚上看星星。其次，许多候鸟能感觉到地球的磁场，就像身体里带着一个“指南针”。此外，河流、高山、海岸等地面上的标志，也能帮助它们确认自己的位置。
不过，近年来，候鸟的长途飞行正面临越来越多的挑战。城市夜晚的灯光会让晚上飞行的候鸟找不到方向；水边草地的减少，也让它们失去了路上休息和寻找食物的地方。保护候鸟，需要人们共同的努力。

tr.en: Lao Zhou is an ordinary secondary-school teacher and also a bird-photography enthusiast of thirty years. Since his youth he has carried his camera all over the hills, riversides and lakesides of his home region, photographing more than two hundred kinds of birds. At first he simply found birds beautiful and wanted to photograph them. But as he went on, he noticed that some once-common birds were becoming rarer, while some never seen before had appeared. "Photos can speak: they record changes in our home's environment," he says. So he began carefully organising his photos, recording the time, place and number of birds each time. These records later caught the attention of the local environmental department and became an important reference for studying the local ecology. Now he often visits schools to tell children about birds. "I hope children learn early that protecting birds is protecting our own home."

老周是一名普通的中学老师，也是一位有三十年经验的鸟类摄影爱好者。从年轻时起，他就背着相机，走遍了家乡的山林、河边和湖边，拍下了两百多种鸟的照片。
最开始，老周只是觉得鸟很美，想把它们拍下来。可是拍着拍着，他发现，有些过去常见的鸟越来越少了，而一些以前从没见过的鸟却出现在了家乡。“照片是会说话的，它们记录了家乡环境的变化。”老周说。
于是，老周开始认真整理照片，记录每次拍摄的时间、地点和鸟的数量。这些资料后来引起了当地环保部门的重视，成为研究本地生态环境的重要参考。
如今，老周还经常到学校给孩子们讲鸟的故事。他说：“我希望孩子们从小就知道，保护鸟类，就是保护我们自己的家园。”

tr.en: In the past many thought buying second-hand was a loss of face. Today that view is changing. More and more young people buy and sell things they no longer use on online second-hand platforms: clothes they don't wear, appliances used only a few times, books they've finished — all find new owners there. The reasons are many. On one hand, second-hand goods are cheap — some almost new for half the original price or less; on the other, selling unused things frees space at home and earns some money. More importantly, many young people feel that making full use of things is itself an environmentally friendly way of life. Of course there are problems: quality is hard to guarantee and disputes between buyer and seller arise easily. Experts suggest the platforms strengthen management and set up better inspection systems so consumers can buy with confidence.

items.text:
以前，很多人觉得买二手东西“没面子”。如今，这种观念正在发生变化。越来越多的年轻人在网上的二手平台买卖自己不再用的物品：不再穿的衣服、只用过几次的电器、看完的书……都能在这里找到新主人。
年轻人喜欢二手交易，原因是多方面的。一方面，二手商品价格便宜，有的几乎是全新的，却只要原价的一半甚至更低；另一方面，把不用的东西卖掉，既能空出家里的空间，又能赚一些钱。更重要的是，很多年轻人认为，让物品得到充分利用，本身就是一种环保的生活方式。
当然，二手交易也存在一些问题，比如商品质量难以保证、买卖双方容易发生纠纷等。专家建议，二手平台应当加强管理，建立更完善的检验制度，让消费者买得放心。

tr.en: A bookmark printed with an ancient painting, a fan bearing a relic's pattern, a box of biscuits shaped like ancient buildings… In recent years the cultural and creative products launched by big museums have grown ever more popular; some sell out as soon as they go on sale. They are popular because they combine history and culture with daily life: once people could only admire relics through glass; now they can take home products with elements of those relics and use them every day. Many young people say it was liking these products that first made them interested in museums and history. But developing them can't just chase looks and sales. Experts point out that a good product should truly tell the story behind the relic, not simply print a pattern on goods; only then can it really help spread traditional culture.

items.text:
一张印着古画的书签，一把有文物图案的扇子，一盒造型像古代建筑的饼干……近年来，各大博物馆推出的文化创意产品越来越受欢迎，有的甚至一上市就卖光了。
博物馆创意产品之所以受欢迎，是因为它们把历史文化和日常生活结合在了一起。过去，人们只能隔着玻璃欣赏文物；现在，人们可以把带着文物元素的产品带回家，在生活中使用。不少年轻人表示，正是因为喜欢这些创意产品，他们才开始对博物馆和历史产生兴趣。
不过，创意产品的开发也不能只追求好看和好卖。有专家指出，好的创意产品应当真正讲好文物背后的故事，而不是简单地把图案印在商品上。只有这样，创意产品才能真正起到传播传统文化的作用。

tr.en: Calligraphy is a unique Chinese art form with thousands of years of history. In ancient times people wrote with brushes, and calligraphy slowly developed in the process. A good piece of calligraphy is not only beautifully written but also shows the writer's character and feelings. Learning it takes great patience: many calligraphers start practising as children, writing several hours a day for decades without giving up. However, now that computers and phones are everywhere, fewer and fewer people write with a brush. To pass the art on better, many schools have opened calligraphy classes, letting pupils encounter traditional culture from an early age.

tr.en: Have you noticed that when you see someone yawn, you can't help yawning too? This is called the "contagion" of yawning. Scientists studying it found that the closer two people are, the more easily yawns "spread": people easily yawn when they see family or close friends do so, but much less when they see strangers. Some research links this to empathy: the better someone understands others' feelings, the more easily they are affected by them. Research also found that children under four are rarely affected, perhaps because their ability to understand others' emotions isn't fully developed. Interestingly, the contagion isn't only between humans: experiments show dogs can "catch" yawns from their owners — when the owner yawns, the dog often follows.

tr.en: On a small street in the old town there is a noodle shop that has been open for forty years. It's small, with only six tables, yet full of customers every day. The owner, surnamed Chen, is now seventy. He gets up at four every morning to make noodles and boil the broth. He has a rule he has kept for forty years: "The broth must boil for six full hours — a minute less and the taste is wrong." In forty years prices have risen only twice; a bowl is still only twelve yuan. People urge him to raise prices or open a few more shops to earn more, but he always smiles and shakes his head: "I didn't open a noodle shop to get rich, but so the neighbours could eat a really good bowl of noodles." Now the little shop has become the "old taste" in many people's hearts: many old neighbours who have moved away make a special trip back for a bowl whenever they return to the old town.

tr.en: In city streets and scenic spots you may see young people in ancient-style clothes: they're wearing hanfu. In recent years hanfu has become more and more popular with young people, and spending on it keeps growing. Hanfu is the traditional dress of the Han people, with thousands of years of history. Compared with modern clothes, its styles, colours and patterns are distinctive and reflect traditional Chinese taste. Many young people say putting on hanfu is like a close encounter with history, which has made them more interested in traditional culture. As it has spread, hanfu-related events have appeared everywhere, such as hanfu culture festivals and hanfu photography; some scenic spots even let visitors in hanfu in free to attract more young people. But some argue that wearing hanfu shouldn't just be for pretty photos — more important is understanding the culture behind it. Only then can the hanfu craze truly last.

走在城市的街头或者景区里，你可能会看到一些穿着古代服装的年轻人。他们穿的就是汉服。近几年，汉服在年轻人中越来越流行，相关的消费也越来越多。
汉服指的是汉族的传统服装，有着几千年的历史。和现代服装相比，汉服的样式、颜色和图案都很有特点，体现了中国传统的审美。很多年轻人表示，穿上汉服，就好像和历史有了一次近距离的接触，这让他们对传统文化产生了更大的兴趣。
随着汉服的流行，各地还出现了不少与汉服有关的活动，比如汉服文化节、汉服摄影等。一些景区甚至规定，穿汉服的游客可以免费参观，以此吸引更多年轻人。
不过，也有人认为，穿汉服不能只是为了拍照好看，更重要的是了解服装背后的文化。只有这样，汉服热才能真正持续下去。

tr.en: In parts of cities such as Beijing and Wuhan, people can already call a taxi with no driver on their phones. Once passengers get in, the car drives itself to the destination, parking, turning and waiting at traffic lights with no human control. A driverless car can drive itself thanks to the equipment installed on it, which acts as its "eyes" and "brain": the eyes watch surrounding vehicles, pedestrians and road conditions; the brain quickly makes judgements from this information, deciding when to speed up and when to brake. Supporters say it can reduce accidents caused by tired or inattentive drivers and lower travel costs. But many worry: what if the equipment fails? Who is responsible in an accident? Experts say that although the technology is developing fast, real widespread use needs more preparation in technology, law and management.

在北京、武汉等城市的一些地区，人们已经可以用手机叫到一辆没有司机的出租车。乘客上车后，汽车会自己开往目的地，自己停车、转弯、等红绿灯，一切都不需要人来操作。
无人驾驶汽车之所以能自己开车，靠的是车上安装的各种设备。这些设备就像汽车的“眼睛”和“大脑”：“眼睛”负责观察周围的车辆、行人和道路情况，“大脑”则根据这些信息迅速做出判断，决定什么时候加速、什么时候刹车。
支持者认为，无人驾驶可以减少因为司机疲劳、不注意而造成的交通事故，还能降低出行的成本。但也有不少人担心：如果设备出了问题怎么办？发生事故时，责任应该由谁来承担？
专家表示，无人驾驶技术虽然发展很快，但要真正普及，还需要在技术、法律和管理等方面做更多的准备。

tr.en: Ten years ago, Liu Ming, working away from home, came back to his village and found the children had nowhere to go after school: they either looked at phones or played by the road. "As a child my greatest wish was to have lots of books, but we were poor and even one book was hard to buy." So he decided to start a library in the village. He took the money he had saved from working away, cleared out two old rooms of his family's house and bought a first batch of two thousand books. On opening day more than thirty children came; some sat there all afternoon. To keep it going he started a book-donation campaign online. Unexpectedly, kind-hearted people from all over the country sent books, and some publishers sent whole boxes of new ones. Today the little village library has over twenty thousand books, and children from several surrounding villages come to read. "Seeing the children reading, I feel it was all worth it," he says.

tr.en: In China red is a very special colour. At the Spring Festival every household pastes up red "fu" characters and hangs red lanterns; at weddings the bride wears red and the new home is decorated in red everywhere; the New Year money given to children goes in red envelopes. The Chinese love of red has a long history: in ancient times people thought red stood for the sun and fire, bringing warmth and light and driving away bad things. Gradually red became a symbol of good fortune and happiness. But red isn't right for every occasion: when someone in the family has died, people generally don't wear red. And writing someone's name in red ink is considered impolite in many places. Today "China red" has become an important symbol of Chinese culture, seen in many designs.

在中国，红色是一种非常特别的颜色。春节的时候，家家户户都会贴红色的“福”字、挂红色的灯笼；结婚的时候，新娘要穿红色的衣服，新房里到处都是红色的装饰；过年给孩子的压岁钱，也要装在红包里。
中国人喜欢红色，有着很长的历史。在古代，人们认为红色代表太阳和火，能给人带来温暖和光明，还能赶走不好的东西。慢慢地，红色就成了吉祥、快乐的象征。
不过，红色在中国并不是在任何场合都合适。比如，家里有人去世的时候，人们一般不会穿红色的衣服。另外，用红色的笔写别人的名字，在很多地方也被认为是不礼貌的。
如今，“中国红”已经成为中国文化的一个重要符号，在很多设计中都能看到它。

tr.en: As living standards rise, more and more Chinese families keep pets. Figures show that in recent years the number of cat and dog owners in Chinese cities keeps growing, and pet-related spending with it, forming what people call the "pet economy". Today pets are treated well: special pet food, pet hospitals when they're ill, someone to look after them when owners are away, even shops that photograph pets and hold their birthdays. Some young people say they can economise on themselves but never hesitate to spend on their pets. Why? Experts suggest that many young people live and work alone in big cities, and pets bring them company and comfort, easing loneliness to some degree; to them a pet is no longer just an animal but a member of the family. But experts also remind people that keeping a pet is a long-term responsibility: before deciding, think clearly whether you have enough time and energy.

随着生活水平的提高，越来越多的中国家庭开始养宠物。数据显示，近年来，中国城市里养猫养狗的人数不断增长，和宠物有关的消费也越来越多，形成了人们常说的“宠物经济”。
如今，宠物的“待遇”可不低：吃的有专门的宠物食品，生病了有宠物医院，主人出门时有人帮忙照顾，甚至还有专门给宠物拍照、过生日的店。一些年轻人表示，自己可以节约一点儿，但在宠物身上花钱从来不犹豫。
为什么年轻人愿意在宠物身上花这么多钱？有专家分析，很多年轻人一个人在大城市工作和生活，宠物能给他们带来陪伴和安慰，在一定程度上减轻了孤独感。对他们来说，宠物早已不只是动物，而是家庭的一员。
不过，专家也提醒，养宠物是一份长期的责任，在决定养宠物之前，一定要想清楚自己是否有足够的时间和精力。

tr.en: Hotpot is one of the Chinese people's favourite foods. One pot, one table of people sitting round it, eating and chatting — very lively. The method is simple too: put meat and vegetables into the boiling broth, and once cooked they're ready to eat. Hotpot differs from place to place: Chongqing hotpot is famous for being spicy, while Beijing hotpot mostly cooks mutton in clear broth. Whichever kind it is, hotpot feels warm and familiar. Today hotpot has gone abroad, and hotpot restaurants can be found all over the world. For many Chinese living abroad, a hotpot meal is all the more a way of missing home.

tr.en: "Early to bed and early to rise is good for you" — many have heard it since childhood. But recent research shows that not everyone is suited to getting up early. Researchers found that sleeping and waking habits depend largely on the body's "biological clock". Some people have the most energy in the morning — "larks"; others only come alive at night — "owls". Force an owl to get up early and they'll be listless all day, and less efficient at work. So experts suggest learning your own body's pattern, finding the sleep times that suit you best, and at the same time making sure you get enough sleep.

“早睡早起身体好”，这是很多人从小就听到的话。不过，最近有研究（　），并不是每个人都适合早起。
研究人员发现，人睡觉和起床的习惯，在很大程度上和身体里的“生物钟”有关。有的人早上精力最好，被称为“百灵鸟型”；有的人却要到了晚上才（　），被称为“猫头鹰型”。如果（　）“猫头鹰型”的人早起，他们反而会一整天没精神，工作效率也会下降。
因此，专家建议，大家应该（　）自己的身体特点，找到最适合自己的睡觉时间，（　）保证充足的睡眠。

tr.en: At half past eleven, the "seniors' canteen" of a Beijing neighbourhood is already full. Most of those who come to eat are old people from nearby. Three dishes and a soup, meat and vegetables, for just over ten yuan a portion. In recent years many cities have opened such community canteens. They mainly solve old people's "eating problem": some live alone and find cooking inconvenient; some have bad teeth and can't eat hard food. Following their needs, the canteens make the food softer and lighter. A community canteen isn't only a place to eat: many old people don't hurry home after their meal but chat about everyday things and play chess, and once-lonely days have become lively. Now some canteens are open to young people too, so that office workers nearby can also have an affordable lunch.

tr.en: Twenty-six-year-old Xiao Lin comes from a small mountain village in Zhejiang, where generation after generation have woven baskets from bamboo. She learnt basket weaving from her grandmother as a child. After university she found a good job in Hangzhou, but seeing fewer and fewer villagers who could weave baskets, she finally chose to go home. Back in the village she found that traditional bamboo baskets, though sturdy and long-lasting, looked plain and hardly appealed to young people. So she combined bamboo weaving with modern design, creating bamboo lamps, phone stands, earrings and other new products. She also opened an online shop, showing how bamboo weaving is done in videos. Many people learnt for the first time that bamboo could become so many beautiful things, and orders grew day by day. Now over twenty old villagers weave with her. Xiao Lin says she hopes this traditional art will be passed on for ever.

tr.en: In the past, as soon as winter came, many tourist sights in northern China had few visitors and business was poor. But in recent years that has changed a lot: ice-and-snow tourism is ever more popular, and winter has become the liveliest season for some northern cities. Take Harbin: every winter it builds "ice cities" from huge blocks of ice — ice houses, ice bridges… At night coloured lights shine on the ice, very beautiful. Visitors come from all over the country and even abroad, some bringing their children specially to see and play in the snow. The growth of ice-and-snow tourism has boosted local hotels, restaurants and transport and given locals many jobs. But winter is bitterly cold and visitors' safety needs special care: the local government has strengthened management of the sights and provided free rest points where everyone can warm up.

items.text:
过去，一到冬天，中国北方的很多旅游景点游客就很少，生意也不好。可是这几年，情况发生了很大的变化。冰雪旅游越来越受欢迎，冬天反而成了北方一些城市最热闹的季节。
以哈尔滨为例，每年冬天，这里都会用巨大的冰块建起一座座“冰城”：冰做的房子、冰做的桥……到了晚上，五颜六色的灯光照在冰上，十分漂亮。来自全国各地甚至国外的游客纷纷前来，有的还专门带着孩子来看雪、玩雪。
冰雪旅游的发展，带动了当地的酒店、餐饮、交通等行业，也为当地人提供了大量的工作机会。不过，冬季天气寒冷，游客的安全问题也需要特别注意。当地政府加强了对景区的管理，还为游客提供了免费的休息点，让大家可以进去暖和一下。

tr.en: Laughter is one of the commonest human expressions. Research finds it not only expresses happiness but also benefits health in many ways. When we laugh, many muscles in the face and body move, and breathing deepens; some research suggests a few minutes of hearty laughter is like a little exercise. Laughter also helps relieve stress and relax tense emotions. It has another interesting feature: it is very "contagious". Studies find people laugh far more with others than alone; often we laugh not because we've heard something funny but to show friendliness and bring each other closer. So some experts suggest spending more time with family and friends and laughing more — good for both body and mind.

items.text:
笑是人类最常见的表情之一。科学研究发现，笑不仅能表达快乐的心情，对身体健康也有很多好处。
人在笑的时候，脸上和身上的很多肌肉都会参与运动，呼吸也会变得更深。有研究认为，大笑几分钟，就好像做了一次简单的运动。此外，笑还能帮助人们减轻压力，让紧张的情绪得到放松。
笑还有一个有趣的特点：它很容易“传染”。研究发现，人和别人在一起时笑的次数，比一个人的时候多得多。在很多情况下，人们笑并不是因为听到了什么好笑的事情，而是为了表达友好，让彼此的关系更近。
因此，有专家建议，人们平时可以多和家人、朋友在一起，多笑一笑，这对身心健康都很有好处。

tr.en: After retiring, sixty-two-year-old Uncle Zhang did something that astonished his family: he decided to travel by bicycle. At first they all objected: "At your age, what if something happens on the road?" But he insisted. To prepare, he started training half a year ahead, cycling twenty or thirty kilometres a day, and learnt to repair bikes. Last spring he set off south from his home province of Shandong. He cycled by day and stayed in small inns at night, writing down in his diary the scenery and the people at each place. In over a year he cycled more than ten thousand kilometres through a dozen provinces. On the way he met many kind people: some treated him to meals, some fixed his bike, and young cyclists rode part of the way with him. "This trip taught me there's no such thing as starting too late. As long as you have a dream, it's never too late to set out."

questions.zh: 「只要有夢想，什麼時候出發都不晚」。
questions.zh-Hans: 「只要有梦想，什么时候出发都不晚」。

items.text:
六十二岁的张大爷退休以后，做了一件让家人都吃惊的事：他决定骑自行车去旅行。
刚开始，家人都反对。“您这么大年纪了，路上要是出点儿事怎么办？”可是张大爷很坚持。为了这次旅行，他提前半年就开始锻炼身体，每天骑车二三十公里，还学会了修自行车。
去年春天，张大爷从家乡山东出发，一路向南。他白天骑车，晚上住在小旅馆里，每到一个地方，都会把看到的风景和遇到的人记在日记本上。一年多的时间里，他骑了一万多公里，经过了十几个省。
旅途中，张大爷遇到了很多热心人：有人请他吃饭，有人帮他修车，还有骑车的年轻人陪他走了一段路。他说：“这次旅行让我明白，人生没有太晚的开始。只要有梦想，什么时候出发都不晚。”

tr.en: In China the "Clean Plate Campaign" has been promoted for many years. It means eating up the food on your plate and not wasting it. In the past, when treating guests, many people felt the more dishes they ordered, the more face they gained, and often left a whole table of food. Surveys show the amount of food wasted at Chinese tables every year is astonishing. To cut waste, many restaurants have come up with ideas: small and half portions so customers can order less and try more; waiters reminding customers to order what they need; takeaway boxes offered for leftovers. Some school and workplace canteens run related campaigns, praising students and staff who clear their plates. Saving food isn't a slogan; it should become everyone's habit. As one expert put it, "Cutting waste starts with every meal."

items.text:
在中国，“光盘行动”已经提倡了很多年。“光盘行动”的意思是，吃饭时把盘子里的饭菜吃光，不浪费食物。
过去，很多人请客吃饭时，觉得点的菜越多越有面子，结果常常剩下一大桌子菜。有调查显示，中国每年在餐桌上浪费的食物数量十分惊人。
为了减少浪费，很多饭馆想出了各种办法：推出“小份菜”“半份菜”，让顾客可以少点一些、多尝几种；服务员会提醒顾客按需要点菜；吃不完的饭菜，饭馆会主动提供打包盒。一些学校和单位的食堂也开展了相关活动，对吃光饭菜的学生和员工进行表扬。
节约粮食不是一句口号，而应该成为每个人的生活习惯。正如一位专家所说：“减少浪费，要从每一顿饭做起。”

tr.en: In parts of north-west China the sky used to be full of yellow sand, and wind and sand greatly affected local life. To change this, for decades the local government and people have kept planting trees and grass, fighting the desert. Planting trees in the desert isn't easy: water is scarce and the wind strong, so young trees are easily blown over or buried in sand. So people came up with a good method: first weave grass into squares on the sand to hold it in place, then plant trees and grass inside the squares. Simple and effective, it greatly raised the share of young trees that survive. After the efforts of several generations, desert in many places has turned green. There is less sand in the wind, the air is better, and locals have developed farming and tourism along the desert's edge, with clearly higher incomes. Their success also offers other countries a reference for controlling deserts.

items.text:
在中国西北部的一些地区，过去常常是黄沙满天，大风和沙子给当地居民的生活带来了很大的影响。为了改变这种情况，几十年来，当地政府和人民坚持种树种草，和沙漠作斗争。
在沙漠里种树并不容易。那里缺水，风又大，刚种下去的小树很容易被风吹倒，或者被沙子埋住。为此，人们想出了一个好办法：先用草在沙地上编成一个个方格，把沙子固定住，然后再在方格里种树种草。这种方法简单有效，大大提高了小树活下来的比例。
经过几代人的努力，很多地方的沙漠变成了一片绿色。大风和沙子少了，空气好了，当地人还在沙漠边上发展起了种植和旅游，收入也有了明显的提高。这些地方的成功经验，也为世界上其他国家治理沙漠提供了参考。
